passage: In the village near Sikar, Yamini decided that sleep was for people who did not want the scholarship test. She set her alarm for 3 a.m., skipped the evening walk to the well with her brother Irfan and ate lunch with the book propped against her plate. By the second week, the formulas she had learnt slid away by afternoon and she read the same paragraph four times. On the mock test she left two easy questions blank, then cried over the paper. Irfan found her on the veranda step. "You look like the lamp when the oil is low," he said. That night she slept until six, and the next day the paragraph made sense in one read.

qa.q: What time did Yamini set her alarm for?
qa.a: Yamini set her alarm for 3 a.m.

qa.q: How was Yamini feeling on the veranda step after the mock test?
qa.a: Upset and frustrated, since she cried over the blank answers even though she was working harder than ever.

qa.q: What could Yamini try to protect her studying?
qa.a: Sleep at regular hours and keep short breaks such as the evening walk, so that what she learns stays with her.

qa.q: How might Irfan see his sister's new routine?
qa.a: With worry; the lamp remark shows he sees her running low on energy.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager preparing for an entrance test who cuts sleep and breaks, then finds memory and concentration falling.

passage: Yosef pinned a note above his bed in Lyon: Wake at 4:30. He had worked out that sleeping until seven cost him two and a half hours a day, and he was not going to lose them before the entrance test in June. He skipped breaks too, eating bread at his desk. After ten days he could not recall the rule he had studied on Monday, and twice he left his keys in the door. In the mock test he wrote the wrong term where the answer needed the discriminant. His study partner Clara pushed the marked paper across the table. "You knew this in March," she said. Yosef felt strangely proud of the tiredness, as if it proved something, but he did not answer, and later set the alarm for six.

qa.q: What time did Yosef's note say to wake?
qa.a: The note said to wake at 4:30.

qa.q: What did Yosef feel about the tiredness even as his marks fell?
qa.a: Strangely proud, as if it proved something, yet uneasy enough to move his alarm to six.

qa.q: What could Yosef do with the extra hours he wants?
qa.a: Protect his sleep and take breaks so that what he studies stays in memory; short rested sessions beat long tired ones.

qa.q: How does Clara see Yosef's studying?
qa.a: With concern; reminding him that he knew the material in March shows she sees the tiredness costing him.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who gives up sleep and breaks for exam hours and sees memory and performance drop while the sacrifice still feels virtuous.

passage:
March. Nikita was preparing for the state engineering entrance exam. She decided sleep was wasted time. She moved her alarm earlier and studied past midnight. Her mother, Sangeeta, found her asleep at the desk twice but said nothing yet.
April. Nikita's mock test scores began to drop. In class, she read the same paragraph four times and couldn't remember it. She forgot formulas she'd known for a year. She felt proud of her tiredness, though, as if it proved she was serious.
May. After a mock where she scored lower than in January, she cried at the kitchen table. Sangeeta sat with her. "You're working more and getting less. Your brain needs the night to store what you learn." They agreed: lights out at a fixed time, one proper break in the afternoon.
June. The next two mocks went up. Nikita still studied hard. She just stopped treating exhaustion as a medal.

qa.q: How did Nikita's mock test scores change in April?
qa.a: Nikita's mock test scores began to drop.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel about being so tired in April?
qa.a: Nikita felt proud of her tiredness, as if it proved she was serious, even while struggling to remember things.

qa.q: What changed after the May conversation, and why did it help?
qa.a: A fixed lights-out time and a proper afternoon break, which let Nikita's concentration and memory recover.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta have felt finding Nikita asleep at the desk?
qa.a: Sangeeta was probably worried, watching quietly until Nikita was ready to talk.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who cuts sleep to gain study hours and finds concentration and memory falling, though the sacrifice feels virtuous.

passage:
Nitin, you're sleeping three hours before your exams? Sit. Your Farida phuphi did the same, and I'll tell you what happened.
My Class Twelve board year, I thought the toppers were the ones who never slept. I studied till two, woke at five. My mother would find me at the desk with my head on the book. I felt so proud of that.
By February I was reading the same page again and again. I'd put down my chemistry notes and couldn't say one thing from them. I snapped at everyone. I once put salt in my tea.
In the pre-board, I blanked on a question I had solved ten times. Ten times, Nitin.
Our chemistry teacher, Mr Rao, saw my paper and called me in. "You're not lazy, Farida. You're exhausted." He made me promise to sleep properly for two weeks.
I did. My marks went up. I felt like I had been cheating myself of the hours I thought I was winning.

qa.q: What did Farida once put in her tea?
qa.a: Salt.

qa.q: How did young Farida feel about sleeping so little at first?
qa.a: Farida felt proud of it, believing toppers were the ones who never slept.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: When Farida blanked in the pre-board and Mr Rao called her in, and she promised to sleep properly for two weeks.

qa.q: How might Mr Rao have felt seeing Farida's pre-board paper?
qa.a: Mr Rao was probably concerned, recognising exhaustion rather than laziness in her mistakes.

grounding: An elder recalls cutting sleep before board exams, feeling virtuous while her memory and concentration fell, until a teacher intervened.

passage:
It was May in Nagpur, and the power went out every afternoon. Shankar, preparing for the maths olympiad, decided to study at night instead, when it was cooler and quieter. He also kept his mornings for school. That left four hours of sleep.
His friend Yash said, "You look terrible." Shankar said, "Toppers don't sleep."
In the second week, he started making silly mistakes: copying numbers wrong, forgetting a sign. He'd sit with a problem for an hour and not see what he'd seen easily a month ago. He blamed the heat.
On the day of the olympiad, the fan in the hall wasn't working. Halfway through, Shankar's eyes closed for a moment. He jerked awake, heart pounding. Ten minutes had gone.
He solved four problems out of six. Yash, who'd slept normally, solved five.
On the bus home, Shankar said quietly, "I thought I was buying hours. I was just borrowing them."

qa.q: How many problems did Shankar solve?
qa.a: He solved four problems out of six.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel when he jerked awake in the exam?
qa.a: Shankar felt a jolt of panic, heart pounding, realising ten minutes had gone.

qa.q: What went wrong with Shankar's plan, and what could he change?
qa.a: Cutting sleep made him slower and error-prone; keeping a full night's sleep and studying in shorter blocks would protect his thinking.

qa.q: How does Yash see Shankar's plan?
qa.a: Yash is worried, telling Shankar he looks terrible, and his own normal sleep gives him a better result.

grounding: Shows a teenager who sacrifices sleep for exam preparation and loses concentration and marks, though the sacrifice felt virtuous.

passage:
In her Hyderabad flat, Sangeeta had moved her alarm to five and her bedtime to past two. The entrance exam was in March; every hour felt like marks. She ate lunch with one hand and held a physics book in the other, and she dropped the evening walk with Afreen.
By the third week things started slipping. In the coaching test she read a question about a pulley three times and still couldn't hold it in her head. She blanked on a formula she had known since class nine. On the bus she dozed off and missed her stop.
"You look like a ghost," Afreen said on the phone.
"I'm fine. I'm just putting in more hours than everyone."
Her test score came back lower than the month before. Sangeeta stared at it, then at the timetable on her wall, where the word "sleep" had been crossed out in red.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta miss when she dozed off on the bus?
qa.a: She missed her stop.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta insist "I'm fine" to Afreen?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt proud of the extra hours and anxious about the exam, so she saw her tiredness as a worthy sacrifice rather than a warning.

qa.q: What small change could help Sangeeta's scores?
qa.a: Putting sleep back on the timetable and keeping the evening walk, so her concentration and memory recover enough to use the hours she studies.

qa.q: How does Afreen see what is happening?
qa.a: Afreen sees that Sangeeta is worn out, saying she looks like a ghost, and is probably worried about her.

grounding: Shows a teenager cutting sleep and breaks for a competitive exam and finding concentration and memory falling.
